title: Drawing Book
directAnswer: A book of n pages can be opened to page p by turning sheets from the front or from the back, and you want the smaller of those two counts. Turning from the front costs p/2 sheets; turning from the back costs n/2 − p/2 sheets. The answer is min(p/2, n/2 − p/2) using integer division. It is O(1) — no loop needed.

remember.pattern: Count from both ends, take the minimum
remember.formula:
front = p / 2
back  = n / 2 - p / 2
return min(front, back)   // integer division throughout
rules: Pages come in **sheets of two**: page 1 is alone on the opening sheet, then 2-3, 4-5, and so on. That is why every count divides by 2.
Sheets to reach page p **from the front** is exactly `p / 2` with integer division — `floor`, never rounding up.
**Total sheets** in the book is `n / 2` (integer division), so sheets from the back is `n / 2 - p / 2`.
Compute both directions and return the **smaller** — the whole problem is one `min` of two integer divisions.
Do **not** simulate page flips in a loop. Reaching for a `while` here signals you missed the closed-form answer.
whenToUse: You can approach a target from two ends and want the cheaper side
Items are grouped in fixed-size chunks (here, two pages per sheet)
The phrase 'minimum number of turns / steps' over a linear layout
An O(1) closed form exists and a loop would only re-derive it
antiSignals: Chunk size varies per step → you actually need a loop or DP
You must return the sequence of turns, not just the count → simulate
The structure is a tree or graph, not a flat line → BFS/DFS instead
Pages are not paired in twos → the /2 assumption breaks
remember.takeaway: When you can reach a target from either end of a fixed structure, the answer is almost always min(distance from front, distance from back). Drawing Book is the cleanest example: two pages per sheet turns the whole thing into min(p/2, n/2 − p/2) with zero looping.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can translate a physical 'flip the book' description into integer arithmetic, correctly model that pages are paired two-per-sheet, and spot the O(1) closed form instead of simulating turns.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting integer (floor) division and treating page 1 as if it shared a sheet with page 2, which shifts every count by one. Or simulating flips in a loop when a formula exists.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the sheet model out loud ('two pages per sheet, page 1 sits alone'), derive front = p/2 and back = n/2 − p/2 from it, and explain why integer division is exactly the floor you want.

problemStatement:
A teacher asks a student to find a specific page `p` in a textbook that has `n` pages. The student can turn sheets from the **front** of the book or from the **back**, whichever is closer.

Each sheet has two pages: page 1 is on the first sheet by itself, then pages 2 and 3 share a sheet, pages 4 and 5 share a sheet, and so on.

Given `n` and `p`, return the **minimum number of sheet turns** needed to arrive at page `p`.
constraints: Each sheet holds exactly two page numbers (except the cover behaviour described)
Turning is counted in whole sheets, never half a sheet
understanding: The book is a stack of sheets, each showing two consecutive page numbers. Because page 1 opens by itself, page p always lands on sheet number p/2 (integer division) counting from the front. The total number of sheets you could ever turn is n/2. So from the front you turn p/2 sheets; from the back you turn the remaining n/2 − p/2. You want whichever is fewer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does turning from the back also cost whole sheet turns?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Both directions are measured in sheets. From the back you turn n/2 − p/2 sheets to land on the same sheet as page p.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How are the pages laid out across sheets?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Two per sheet: 1 alone on the opening sheet, then (2,3), (4,5), (6,7)... That pairing is exactly why every count divides by two.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the division floor or rounded?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Floor — plain integer division. Page 3 and page 2 both sit on sheet 1 (3/2 = 1, 2/2 = 1), so you must truncate, not round up.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can n be odd?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. If n is odd the last sheet shows a single page, but n/2 with integer division still gives the correct total sheet count from the back.

examples.explanation: From the front: turn 1 sheet to reach the 2-3 sheet. From the back: 3 − 1 = 2 sheets. min(1, 2) = 1.
From the front: 4/2 = 2 sheets. From the back: 5/2 − 2 = 0 sheets — page 4 is already on the last sheet. min(2, 0) = 0.
From the front: 3/2 = 1 sheet. From the back: 7/2 − 1 = 2 sheets. min(1, 2) = 1.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree. Drawing Book lives on the 'reachable from both ends, fixed chunk size' branch — pure formula.

approaches.name: Simulation — Flip Sheets One at a Time
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly as the literal reading of the prompt, then replace it with the formula to show you can collapse the loop.
hints: The most literal model: start looking at the opening sheet and flip forward one sheet at a time until page p appears on the visible spread. Count the flips.
After `t` flips from the front, the visible pages are 2t and 2t+1. So you stop flipping the moment 2t+1 is no longer less than p.
Once you know the front count, the back count is total sheets minus front: n/2 − front. Return the smaller of the two.
approaches.complexityReasoning: In the worst case page p is near the middle, so the loop runs about p/2 ≈ n/4 times — linear in n. Only a couple of counters are stored, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
This is the version you would act out with a real book: open to the first sheet, then turn forward one sheet at a time, counting, until page `p` is staring back at you.

**Modelling a single flip.** After `t` flips from the front, the spread in front of you shows pages `2t` and `2t+1`. The opening sheet (`t = 0`) shows page 1 on the right. The next flip (`t = 1`) shows pages 2 and 3, and so on. Page `p` is visible exactly when `2t <= p <= 2t+1`, so you keep flipping while the right-hand page `2t+1` is still less than `p`.

**Deriving the back count without a second loop.** The book has `n / 2` sheets you could turn in total. If reaching `p` from the front took `front` flips, then reaching the same sheet from the back takes the leftover sheets: `n/2 − front`. You do not need to simulate the back separately — the two counts are complementary.

**Why this is the version you replace.** The loop runs up to about `n/4` times, which for `n = 10⁵` is tens of thousands of iterations to compute a number you can write in closed form. It is correct, but every iteration is re-deriving `p / 2` the slow way. Mention it to show you understand the mechanics, then collapse it.
approaches.insight: The front loop is just computing `p / 2` one increment at a time, and the back count is the complement `n/2 − p/2`. Seeing that the loop has a closed form is the whole point — say it, then delete the loop.

dryRun.intro: Flip forward from the opening sheet, counting, until page 2 is on the visible spread.

steps.action: visible pages = 2,3; right page 3 is not < 2 → stop

java.explanation: After `front` flips the right-hand page is 2*front+1; keep flipping while p is still further on.
Total sheets is n/2; the back count is whatever is left after the front flips.
Take the cheaper side — the answer is always the smaller of the two counts.

python.explanation: The right-hand visible page after `front` flips is 2*front+1; stop once p is reached.
Integer-divide total pages by 2 for total sheets, then subtract the front flips.
Return the smaller of the two directions.

diagrams.title: Flipping forward one sheet at a time
diagrams.caption: Each node is a spread; the loop stops when page p first appears.

pitfalls: Looping at all — this O(n) walk only re-derives p/2 the slow way.
Stopping the loop one flip late by comparing the left page (2*front) instead of the right page (2*front+1).
Computing the back count with a second, separate loop instead of the complement n/2 − front.

approaches.name: Direct Formula — min(p/2, n/2 − p/2) (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the sheet model, then state the closed form and that it is O(1).
hints: You never need to flip. The sheet that holds page p is fixed: it is sheet number p/2 counting from the front (integer division).
The book has n/2 sheets total, so the same sheet sits n/2 − p/2 turns away from the back.
The answer is just the smaller of those two distances: min(p/2, n/2 − p/2). No loop, two divisions and a min.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two integer divisions, one subtraction, one comparison — a constant amount of work regardless of n. O(1) time and O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Skip the flipping entirely and compute the two distances directly.

**Why page p lives on sheet p/2.** Because page 1 opens alone, the pairing runs 1 | 2-3 | 4-5 | 6-7. Integer division by 2 maps every page to its sheet: 1/2 = 0, 2/2 = 1, 3/2 = 1, 4/2 = 2, 5/2 = 2. The floor is doing real work here — pages 2 and 3 must collapse to the same sheet, which only happens if you truncate rather than round. So the sheets you turn from the front to reach page p is exactly `p / 2`.

**Why the back distance is n/2 − p/2.** The total number of sheets you could ever turn, front to back, is `n / 2` (integer division, which correctly handles an odd final page). If page p is `p/2` sheets in from the front, then it is the complement, `n/2 − p/2`, sheets in from the back. The two distances always sum to the total sheet count.

**Why the minimum is the answer.** You are free to start from whichever cover is closer, so you take the smaller of the front and back distances. That is the entire algorithm: `min(p/2, n/2 − p/2)`.

**Why this beats the loop.** It produces the same number in three arithmetic operations instead of up to n/4 iterations. For an interview, writing the closed form signals that you modelled the structure instead of brute-forcing it.
approaches.insight: The front distance and back distance are complements that sum to n/2, so once you have one you get the other for free. The floor in `p / 2` is not a rounding convenience — it is the exact operation that pairs two pages onto one sheet.

dryRun.intro: No flipping — compute both distances with integer division and take the minimum.

java.explanation: Integer division floors page p to its sheet index counting from the front.
Total sheets n/2 minus the front distance gives the distance from the back.
Whichever cover is closer wins — return the smaller count.

python.explanation: Floor division maps page p onto its sheet from the front.
Total sheets minus the front distance is the back distance.
Return the smaller of the two directions.

diagrams.title: Front distance vs back distance
diagrams.caption: The target sheet splits the book; you take whichever side is shorter.

edgeCases.behavior: from_front = 0, total sheets = 0, from_back = 0. min(0, 0) = 0 — the page is already open.
from_front = 2, total sheets = 2, from_back = 0 → 0. The last page is reached instantly from the back.
from_front = 1, total sheets = 2, from_back = 1 → min(1, 1) = 1. Both sides tie; either works.

pitfalls: Using floating-point or rounding division instead of integer floor — pages 2 and 3 must collapse onto the same sheet.
Computing total sheets as (n+1)/2 or n − 1 instead of n/2 — only n/2 matches the pairing.
Returning the front distance alone and forgetting the book can be opened from the back.

commonMistakes: Rounding p/2 up instead of flooring it, which puts page 3 on the wrong sheet.
Simulating page flips in a loop when the answer is a one-line formula.
Forgetting the back direction and returning only p/2.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Rounding instead of flooring
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Pages 2 and 3 share sheet 1. Only integer (floor) division collapses both onto sheet 1; rounding up sends page 3 to sheet 2 and shifts every count.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: from_front = math.ceil(p / 2)   # page 3 wrongly lands on sheet 2
commonMistakesDetailed.good: from_front = p // 2            # floor: pages 2 and 3 both map to sheet 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Looping when a formula exists
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Walking sheet by sheet is O(n) and only re-derives p/2. The interviewer is checking whether you see the closed form.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int front = 0;
while (2 * front + 1 < p) front++;   // O(n) re-derivation of p/2
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int front = p / 2;                   // O(1) closed form

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong total-sheet count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The book has n/2 sheets. Using n − 1 or (n+1)/2 breaks the back distance, especially when n is odd.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int back = n / 2 - p / 2;     // n/2 is the true sheet count

patternNote: Reach-from-both-ends with a fixed chunk size. Whenever a target on a linear structure can be approached from either side and each step covers a constant amount, the answer collapses to min(distance from front, distance from back). Here two pages per sheet gives min(p/2, n/2 − p/2) in O(1).
